explanations.explanation: A yoke, made from leather straps and worn on Jeremiah's own neck (Jeremiah 27:2). The LORD doesn't just hand him words. He hands him something to wear. I think that's an outfit people would stop and ask about.
Not a sling, friend. The LORD says a yoke, and it goes on Jeremiah's neck, not in his hand. A sling is for throwing. This thing is for wearing, and everybody is going to see it.

You've got the leather right, but a belt goes around the waist. The LORD says a yoke, and Jeremiah puts it on his neck. Walk into a room with that on and nobody's asking where you got your belt. They're asking what on earth is happening up there.

The envoys are standing right there in Jerusalem, so Jeremiah sends the word through them to their kings. Verse 4 says it's a message for them to relay to their masters. It's a delivery with built-in delivery guys, and the kings of Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre and Sidon are the ones getting it.

Babylon's king is who the message is about, not who it goes to. The LORD tells Jeremiah to send word to the kings of Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre and Sidon. The envoys carry it home to those masters (Jeremiah 27:3-4). Nobody is mailing anything to Babylon here.

Judah's elders aren't named in this verse. The word goes to the kings of the five nations, through the envoys who came to Jerusalem to see Zedekiah. Those envoys are the ones who will relay it to their masters. I think they came expecting meetings and left with homework.

God says, "I give it to whom I please." He made the earth, so the giving is His to do (Jeremiah 27:5). Nobody wins it by flexing and nobody gets it by being quick. It's His land, and He decides who gets it.
God never says the strongest gets it. He says He gives the earth to whom He pleases (Jeremiah 27:5). The one who made it gets to decide, not the biggest army. Muscle doesn't get a vote.

No early-bird special on the earth, friend. God says He gives it to whom He pleases (Jeremiah 27:5). Showing up first with your hand out doesn't change that. When you're the one who made it, you get to choose.

Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. God says He has placed all these lands under his authority (Jeremiah 27:6). That's a lot of lands for one man to be put over. I think that man needs a very big calendar.

Pharaoh Neco was a king of Egypt, but this passage never mentions him. God places the lands under Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon (Jeremiah 27:6). The envoys and their kings are hearing about Babylon, and that's where the message points.

Cyrus was the king of Persia, but he isn't in this message. The LORD puts these lands under the authority of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon (Jeremiah 27:6). That's who the five kings need to hear about, and Babylon is where this one is heading.

Not forever. God says the nations will serve Nebuchadnezzar, his son and his grandson, until the time of his own land comes (Jeremiah 27:7). Then many nations and great kings will enslave him. The empire has a stopping point and God has already named it.

Right, it's false. God says the nations will serve Nebuchadnezzar and his son and grandson, until the time of his own land comes (Jeremiah 27:7). After that, many nations and great kings will enslave him. Even the top spot comes with an end date.

True, and it's a heavy one. God says any nation that won't serve Nebuchadnezzar or place its neck under his yoke will be punished by sword and famine and plague (Jeremiah 27:8). It goes on until He has destroyed that nation by his hand. This is the LORD speaking, and the warning is plain.

This one is true, friend, and it's heavy. God says the nation that doesn't serve Nebuchadnezzar and doesn't place its neck under his yoke will be punished by sword and famine and plague (Jeremiah 27:8). He says it goes on until He has destroyed it by his hand. The words are plain, so I'll leave them plain.

Destroyed. God says He'll punish that nation until He has destroyed it by Nebuchadnezzar's hand (Jeremiah 27:8). It's a heavy line, and it shows how serious the warning is. The yoke is the way out of it.

The text doesn't say forgiven. God says He'll punish the nation that refuses until He has destroyed it by Nebuchadnezzar's hand (Jeremiah 27:8). It's a heavy verse. The way out He gives is the yoke, which He lays out in the verses that follow.

Warned is a gentle word, but it isn't the one God uses. The text says He'll punish that nation until He has destroyed it by Nebuchadnezzar's hand (Jeremiah 27:8). The warning is the message itself, and this is what it says will happen if the nation refuses.

explanations.answer: You will not serve Babylon's king
explanations.explanation: Every voice in that crowd is declaring that they will not serve the king of Babylon (Jeremiah 27:9). It sounds nice to hear, and I'm sure it was popular. But the LORD tells them not to listen. Same pitch from every direction doesn't make it true.

explanations.answer: You must flee down to Egypt
explanations.explanation: Egypt never comes up in this verse. What they declare is, 'You will not serve the king of Babylon' (Jeremiah 27:9). It's a comfortable message, and God tells the people not to listen. Nobody's packing for a trip anywhere in this verse.

explanations.answer: Your gods will fight for you
explanations.explanation: Nothing about gods fighting shows up in this verse. The prophets, diviners and sorcerers declare that you will not serve the king of Babylon (Jeremiah 27:9). God tells the people not to listen to any of them. Whatever they're selling, He says don't buy it.

A lie. God says they prophesy a lie that will serve to remove their listeners from their land (Jeremiah 27:10). Then He says He will banish them and they will perish. A lie that sounds good is still a lie, and this one costs people their home.

I know some messages come with a catchy tune, but God doesn't call it a song. He calls it a lie, one that will serve to remove people from their land (Jeremiah 27:10). It might sound pleasant going in. The cost comes later.

There's no puzzle to solve here, friend. God says plainly that they prophesy a lie, and it will serve to remove people from their land (Jeremiah 27:10). He isn't hiding the meaning. He's telling them what it is.

True. God says the nation that puts its neck under the yoke of the king of Babylon and serves him will be left in its own land (Jeremiah 27:11). It will cultivate the land and live in it. After all that warning, here's the kind part: the yoke comes with a home.

This one is true. God says the nation that puts its neck under Babylon's yoke and serves him will be left in its own land, to cultivate it and live in it (Jeremiah 27:11). That's the promise at the end of the warning. The yoke keeps them home.

Live. Jeremiah tells Zedekiah and his people to put their necks under the yoke, serve, and live (Jeremiah 27:12). Right in the middle of the hard message is the word live. It's the goal of the whole thing.

Waiting isn't what Jeremiah says. He tells them to put their necks under the yoke, serve, and live (Jeremiah 27:12). Doing nothing is the one thing he won't let them settle for. The word he ends on is live.

Prayer is a good thing, but it isn't the word Jeremiah uses here. He says to put their necks under the yoke of the king of Babylon, serve him and his people, and live (Jeremiah 27:12). The message is about what they do and what they get. Live is the word.

It's the other way around. Jeremiah tells Zedekiah not to listen to the prophets who say he must not serve the king of Babylon (Jeremiah 27:14). He says they are prophesying a lie. That's about as clear as it gets.

False, and Jeremiah couldn't be plainer. He says do not listen to the words of the prophets who say you must not serve the king of Babylon (Jeremiah 27:14). He says they are prophesying a lie. Some advice you take. This one you leave alone.

Sent. The LORD says He has not sent them, and yet they are prophesying falsely in His name (Jeremiah 27:15). They're using His name, but they're not on His errand. Using the name isn't the same as being sent.

Warned isn't the word the LORD uses. He says He has not sent them, and yet they prophesy falsely in His name (Jeremiah 27:15). The problem isn't what He told them. He never sent them in the first place.

The LORD doesn't say anything about answering them here. He says He has not sent them, yet they are prophesying falsely in His name (Jeremiah 27:15). They show up with a message He never gave them. That's the whole issue.

explanations.answer: They'll be brought back very soon
explanations.explanation: That's what those prophets say: very soon now the articles will be brought back from Babylon (Jeremiah 27:16). Jeremiah calls it a lie. It's the kind of news everybody wants to hear. The LORD says it isn't so, and that settles it.

explanations.answer: They'll be melted down in Babylon
explanations.explanation: That isn't the prophets' message. They say the articles will be brought back from Babylon very soon (Jeremiah 27:16). Jeremiah answers that they're prophesying a lie. Their story is a happy one, and that's why people liked it.

explanations.answer: They'll be sold off to Egypt
explanations.explanation: Egypt isn't in this verse. The prophets say the articles from the house of the LORD will be brought back from Babylon very soon (Jeremiah 27:16). Jeremiah tells the people it's a lie. Good-sounding news can still be false.

A ruin. Jeremiah says to serve the king of Babylon and live, and then he asks why this city should become a ruin (Jeremiah 27:17). It's a real question from a man who wants them to choose well. The way to avoid it is right there in the sentence before.

Prison isn't the word. Jeremiah says serve the king of Babylon and live, then asks why this city should become a ruin (Jeremiah 27:17). He's asking them to think about what's at stake for the whole city.

Battlefield isn't the word Jeremiah picks. He tells them to serve the king of Babylon and live, then asks why this city should become a ruin (Jeremiah 27:17). A ruin is what's on the line. He'd rather they hear him now than see it later.

explanations.answer: That the articles still left stay put
explanations.explanation: That's the challenge. If they're prophets and the word of the LORD is with them, let them plead that the articles remaining in the LORD's house, the king's palace and Jerusalem not be taken to Babylon (Jeremiah 27:18). Jeremiah isn't asking them for more promises. He's asking them to plead for the things that are still there.

That's not the plea Jeremiah names. He says let them plead with the LORD of Hosts that the articles remaining in the LORD's house, the palace and Jerusalem not be taken to Babylon (Jeremiah 27:18). The test is about the things still left in the city.

explanations.answer: That the yoke on Judah breaks
explanations.explanation: Breaking a yoke isn't what Jeremiah says to plead for. He says to plead with the LORD of Hosts that the articles remaining in the house of the LORD, the palace and Jerusalem not be taken to Babylon (Jeremiah 27:18). The challenge is about what's still left in the city.

Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim, a king of Judah. Nebuchadnezzar carried him into exile from Jerusalem to Babylon (Jeremiah 27:20). The pillars, the sea, the bases and the rest were left behind when that happened.

Hezekiah son of Ahaz was a king of Judah (2 Kings 18:1), but he isn't the one in this verse. The text says Nebuchadnezzar carried Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim into exile (Jeremiah 27:20). That's when these articles were left behind.

Josiah is Zedekiah's father, according to the first verse of this chapter (Jeremiah 27:1), but he isn't who's carried off here. The text says Nebuchadnezzar carried Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim into exile (Jeremiah 27:20). The articles stayed behind when he went.

True. When Nebuchadnezzar carried Jeconiah into exile from Jerusalem to Babylon, he took along all the nobles of Judah and Jerusalem (Jeremiah 27:20). It's a heavy part of the story. Jeconiah didn't go alone.

It's true, friend. The text says Nebuchadnezzar carried Jeconiah into exile from Jerusalem to Babylon, along with all the nobles of Judah and Jerusalem (Jeremiah 27:20). It's a heavy part of the story. Jeconiah wasn't the only one taken.

Babylon. The LORD of Hosts says the articles that remain in the house of the LORD, in the king's palace and in Jerusalem will be carried there (Jeremiah 27:22). That's the opposite of what the prophets promised. Jeremiah isn't giving the popular answer.

Egypt isn't where they go. The LORD of Hosts says the articles still in the house of the LORD, the palace and Jerusalem will be carried to Babylon (Jeremiah 27:22). That's where all of this has been pointing.

Tyre is one of the five nations whose envoys came to Jerusalem (Jeremiah 27:3), but it isn't where the articles go. The LORD of Hosts says they will be carried to Babylon (Jeremiah 27:22). Babylon is where this passage keeps landing.

Not for good. The LORD says the articles will be carried to Babylon and remain there until the day He attends to them again (Jeremiah 27:22). Then He says He will bring them back and restore them to this place. Babylon isn't the last word on them.

False, and this is the hopeful part. The LORD says the articles will remain in Babylon until the day He attends to them again (Jeremiah 27:22). Then He says, 'I will bring them back and restore them to this place.' They go, but they don't stay lost.
